title: Friction, Drag and Elasticity
learning_objectives: Compute the kinetic and static friction forces and know which one applies.
Explain what drag is and how it depends on speed.
Relate stress and strain in a material, and use Hooke's law.

sections.title: Introduction: Further Applications of Newton's Laws
objectives: Describe how friction, drag and elasticity each enter Newton's laws.

misconceptions.claim: Newton's second law is the last word on any force.
misconceptions.correction: It is the rule that connects the forces to the motion. Friction, drag and elasticity are three of the forces it is applied to.

summary: Newton's second law applies to any force, once the force is known.
This chapter takes three of them: friction, drag and the force in a spring.
Each one resists motion, and each one has its own rule.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Friction
objectives: Tell static friction from kinetic friction and compute the friction force.
Use the coefficient of friction with the normal force.

misconceptions.claim: Friction is always the same force, whatever the weight on the surface.
misconceptions.correction: The maximum static friction is proportional to the normal force, so a heavier object presses harder and the friction limit rises with it.

summary: Static friction adjusts itself up to a limit, then the object slides.
Kinetic friction has a steady value once the object is sliding.
Both are set by the normal force and the coefficient of friction.

authored_exercises.stem: A box slides to the right across a floor. In which direction does kinetic friction act on the box?
authored_exercises.answer: To the left, opposite to the sliding motion.
solution: Kinetic friction acts between surfaces that slide past each other.
The box slides right, so the friction on it points left.

sections.title: Drag Forces
objectives: Explain what drag is and how it grows with speed.
Sketch the drag force against speed for low and for high speed.

misconceptions.claim: Drag is a small force that only matters for very fast objects.
misconceptions.correction: At low speeds the drag grows with the square of the speed, so doubling the speed quadruples it. It matters for anything that moves through air at speed.

misconceptions.claim: Drag is a small force that only matters at very high speed.
misconceptions.correction: At low speeds the drag grows with the square of the speed, so it matters for anything that moves quickly through air.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the drag as negligible.

summary: Drag opposes the motion and always points against the velocity.
At low speeds the drag is small and grows with the square of the speed.
At high speeds the drag grows faster still.

authored_exercises.stem: As a falling object speeds up, what happens to the acceleration caused by air drag?
authored_exercises.answer: The drag force grows, so the net downward force and the acceleration decrease.
solution: The net force is weight minus drag, so it decreases as drag grows.
The acceleration therefore decreases, and becomes zero at terminal velocity.

sections.title: Elasticity: Stress and Strain
objectives: Define stress and strain, and use Hooke's law for a spring.
Tell the elastic limit, the yield point and the breaking point apart.

misconceptions.claim: A spring stretches a little and then springs back, no matter how hard you pull.
misconceptions.correction: Not past the elastic limit. Beyond it the material does not return to its original shape, and beyond the breaking point it fails altogether.

misconceptions.claim: A spring returns to its original length however hard it is pulled.
misconceptions.correction: Not past the elastic limit. Beyond it the material does not return to its shape.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-5, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the unlimited stretch as an option.

summary: Stress is force over area. Strain is the change in length over the original length.
Hooke's law holds while the material stays in the elastic region.
The elastic limit, the yield point and the breaking point mark three different failures.

authored_exercises.stem: State Hooke’s law in words for a stretched spring.
authored_exercises.answer: Within the elastic limit, the extension is directly proportional to the applied force.
solution: Hooke’s law applies while the spring returns to its original shape.
The extension is the change in length.
Force is proportional to extension: F = kx.

definition.text: The friction force that acts on a body at rest, between zero and the maximum the surface allows.
The friction force on a body that is sliding, proportional to the normal force.
The contact force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself, which sets the size of the friction force.
The resistive force a fluid exerts on a body moving through it, always opposite to the motion.
The force per unit area applied to a material.
The fractional change in length of a material under stress.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Weight is the force that opposes an object sliding on a surface.
exam_traps.correction: The force that opposes sliding is the frictional force. Weight is the pull of the Earth, and it acts downward.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the weight as an option in a question asking for the force that opposes sliding.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The coefficient of friction is the acceleration of the sliding body.
exam_traps.correction: The coefficient of friction is a ratio between the friction force and the normal force. It has no units, while an acceleration does.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the acceleration from the question as an option, and the answer is a different number.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The force needed to move a body up an incline is the friction alone.
exam_traps.correction: Moving up the slope, both friction and the down-slope component of the weight oppose the motion, so the applied force must overcome both.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the friction alone as an option, and the answer is the friction plus the component of the weight.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The normal force on a 20 kg block resting on a horizontal table is 200 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. What is the kinetic friction force on the block while it slides?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The kinetic friction is f = μN = 0.3 × 200 = 60 N.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A spring of stiffness 200 N/m is stretched by 5 cm. What is the restoring force in the spring?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Hooke's law gives F = kx = 200 × 0.05 = 10 N.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A body slides on a horizontal surface at constant speed. The horizontal force applied to it is

options.text: equal in magnitude to the friction force

exam_recall_checks.explanation: Constant speed means the net force is zero, so the applied force balances the friction exactly.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The force needed to stretch a spring to twice its extension is
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Hooke's law gives F = kx, so the force is proportional to the extension.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A car travels at 20 m/s and then at 40 m/s. How many times larger is the drag force?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The drag grows with the square of the speed, so doubling the speed makes it four times as large.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A spring is stretched and then released. What happens if it is stretched past its elastic limit?

options.text: It returns to its original length
It stays stretched and does not return

exam_recall_checks.explanation: Past the elastic limit the material does not return to its original shape, so it stays stretched.

sec-4:exr-130.stem: A tightrope walker created a tension of $3.94×10^{3}N$ in a wire making an angle $5.0º$ below the horizontal with each supporting pole. Calculate how much this tension stretches the steel wire if it was originally 15 m long and 0.50 cm in diameter. Take the Young's modulus of steel as $210×10^{9}N/m^{2}$ .

sec-4:exr-106.stem: (a) By how much does a 65.0-kg mountain climber stretch her 0.800-cm diameter nylon rope when the climber hangs 35.0 m below a rock outcropping? Take the Young's modulus of nylon as $5.0×10^{9}N/m^{2}$ . (b) Does the answer seem consistent with what you have observed for nylon ropes? Would it make sense if the rope were actually a bungee cord?

sec-4:exr-111.stem: As an oil well is drilled, each new section of drill pipe supports its own weight and that of the pipe and drill bit beneath it. Calculate the stretch in a new 6.00 m length of steel pipe that supports 3.00 km of pipe having a mass of 20.0 kg/m and a 100-kg drill bit. The pipe is equivalent in stiffness to a solid cylinder 5.00 cm in diameter. Take the Young's modulus of steel as $210×10^{9}N/m^{2}$ .

sec-4:exr-115.stem: A vertebra is subjected to a shearing force of 500 N. Find the shear deformation, taking the vertebra to be a cylinder 3.00 cm high and 4.00 cm in diameter. Take the shear modulus of bone as $80×10^{9}N/m^{2}$ .

sec-4:exr-119.stem: When using a pencil eraser, you exert a vertical force of 6.00 N at a distance of 2.00 cm from the hardwood-eraser joint. The pencil is 6.00 mm in diameter and is held at an angle of $20.0º$ to the horizontal. Take the Young's modulus of hardwood as $15×10^{9}N/m^{2}$ and its shear modulus as $10×10^{9}N/m^{2}$ . (a) By how much does the wood flex perpendicular to its length? (b) How much is it compressed lengthwise?

sec-4:exr-125.answer: 3.6×10^{6}N/m^{2}, which is 360 N/cm^{2} (about 36 atm), so the bottle will not survive.
solution: $3.6×10^{6}N/m^{2}=360N/cm^{2}$, about 36 atm, which is greater than a typical jar can withstand.
